sentences.text: The only known specimen of Juravenator is a juvenile individual measuring about 75 centimeters in length.
This small bipedal predator represents a significant find for understanding early dinosaur evolution.
The four front teeth of the premaxilla had serrations on the upper third of their back edges.
The holotype specimen possessed eight maxillary teeth.
The zygapophyses in the middle of the tail were bow-shaped.
Fossilized skin from the tail and lower hind leg shows normal dinosaur scales alongside traces of what may be simple feathers.
Researchers interpreted small round structures on the tail as integumentary sense organs similar to those of crocodiles, which would be the first such organs found in dinosaur skin.
Small rounded stones interpreted as ooids were found within the belly area of the Juravenator specimen.
The fossil was discovered during a 1998 paleontological expedition organized by the Jura-Museum Eichstätt at the Schamhaupten chalk quarry.
In the summer of 1998, a paleontological expedition was organized by the Jura-Museum Eichstätt at the nearby Schamhaupten chalk quarry.
Initial preparation revealed the head of a small theropod.
The Juravenator specimen was found in almost complete articulation, with only the skull, pelvic girdle, and front tail section partially disarticulated.
Comparisons of scleral rings suggest Juravenator may have been nocturnal, though this might be due to the specimen being a juvenile.
Juravenator may have used these sensory organs to detect aquatic prey like fish while wading in water.
Fossils of isopods found with the specimen suggest they scavenged the carcass while it was floating.
Researchers debated whether the isopods found with Juravenator scavenged the carcass or parasitized the living animal.
Juravenator starki was formally named and described in 2006 by Ursula Göhlich and Luis Chiappe.
The genus Juravenator was named by Göhlich and Chiappe in 2006.
The species Juravenator starki was named by Göhlich and Chiappe in 2006.
Some studies classify Juravenator as a basal member of Maniraptora rather than a compsognathid.
A 2013 analysis classified Juravenator as a coelurosaur closely related to but not part of Compsognathidae, placing it near Ornitholestes outside Maniraptoriformes.
Juravenator belongs to the parent group Coelurosauria.
Juravenator lived approximately 152 to 151 million years ago in the Late Jurassic period in the Franconian Jura of Germany.
Juravenator lived in what is now Germany during the Late Jurassic period.
Juravenator lived approximately 150 million years ago during the Kimmeridgian stage of the Late Jurassic.
Juravenator lived during the Kimmeridgian stage, from 152.21 to 149.2 million years ago.
There is an ongoing debate regarding whether compsognathids belong within Maniraptora or represent a more primitive group.
